title: 1 Chronicles 3:10–24
context: The royal line is now carried from Solomon through the kings of Judah and into the generations after the exile. Verses 10–16 run from Rehoboam to Josiah’s sons and to Jeconiah and Zedekiah, a name-chain rather than a retelling of the reigns already drafted from 1–2 Kings. Differences of naming should be reported, not harmonized: Abijah here is Abijam in 1 Kings 15; Joram here is Jehoram in Kings; Azariah here is also called Uzziah in 2 Kings 15; Jeconiah here is Jehoiachin in 2 Kings 24. Josiah’s sons are listed as Johanan the firstborn, then Jehoiakim, Zedekiah, and Shallum; Kings narrates Jehoahaz, Jehoiakim, and Zedekiah as kings after Josiah, and Shallum is often identified with Jehoahaz, a common reading that should remain hedged. Verse 16 names Jeconiah and Zedekiah as sons of Jehoiakim; whether that Zedekiah is the later king, listed in a dynastic sense, or another son of the same name, is not settled by the wording. From verse 17 the list enters the generation of “Jeconiah, the captive” and then names that are widely read as post-exilic, including Zerubbabel. This chapter calls Zerubbabel a son of Pedaiah, while other books (for example Ezra and Haggai) call him son of Shealtiel; the difference should be named and left standing. Identifications among the later names in 3:17–24 should be hedged. Verse 21 is difficult in the WEB’s wording: after Pelatiah and Jeshaiah, sons of Hananiah, it lists “the sons of Rephaiah, the sons of Arnan, the sons of Obadiah, the sons of Shecaniah” without a clear father-to-son chain. Verse 22 then says the sons of Shemaiah are six and names five men; those features are noted as difficulties of the wording. Both traditions take the unit as the Chronicler’s way of carrying David’s royal line through the kingdom and beyond the exile, still inside the families with which the book began.

verses.text: Solomon’s son was Rehoboam, Abijah his son, Asa his son, Jehoshaphat his son,
verses.arminianNotes:
Solomon’s son is Rehoboam, then Abijah, Asa, and Jehoshaphat. The four open the Judahite royal chain and correspond to the first kings of Judah after Solomon in 1 Kings 12–15 and 22, already drafted in this worktree. Here the name is Abijah; 1 Kings 15 uses Abijam for the same place in the succession. The difference of spelling should be named, not erased.

Arminian readers take the four as a historical succession, the royal line stated as names rather than as reigns.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also point to the drafted Kings narrative as the parallel and leave Abijah and Abijam as the two books’ own forms of the name.

Both traditions trace the royal line as the Chronicler gives it, name the Kings parallel without forcing every spelling or family link into one form, and leave uncertain identifications in the later names openly hedged.

verses.text: Joram his son, Ahaziah his son, Joash his son,
verses.arminianNotes:
The chain continues: “Joram his son, Ahaziah his son, Joash his son,” In Kings the first of these is commonly Jehoram, a longer form of the same royal name; Ahaziah and Joash follow in 2 Kings 8–12. The parallel is that history, already drafted; this verse only lists the sons.

Arminian readers report Joram and Jehoram as a difference of form and still follow the same three-reign sequence.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise name the Kings parallel without requiring one official spelling. The royal line is being carried name by name.

Both traditions trace the royal line as the Chronicler gives it, name the Kings parallel without forcing every spelling or family link into one form, and leave uncertain identifications in the later names openly hedged.

verses.text: Amaziah his son, Azariah his son, Jotham his son,
verses.arminianNotes:
“Amaziah his son, Azariah his son, Jotham his son,” Amaziah, Azariah, and Jotham follow in 2 Kings 14–15. The drafted notes on 2 Kings 15:1–7 already state that Azariah is also called Uzziah in that chapter and in Chronicles’ later narrative. This verse uses Azariah only.

Arminian readers keep the name as this list has it, while acknowledging the other form already recognized in the Kings notes.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also refuse to treat Azariah and Uzziah as a conflict to be solved here. The parallel is 2 Kings 14–15, and the chain continues.

Both traditions trace the royal line as the Chronicler gives it, name the Kings parallel without forcing every spelling or family link into one form, and leave uncertain identifications in the later names openly hedged.

verses.text: Ahaz his son, Hezekiah his son, Manasseh his son,
verses.arminianNotes:
“Ahaz his son, Hezekiah his son, Manasseh his son,” The three match the succession in 2 Kings 16–21, already drafted, where their reigns are told at length. Here they are only names in the royal line.

Arminian readers take the verse as a historical link, not a judgment scene; the moral evaluations of those kings belong to Kings and to later chapters of this book.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same restraint. The Chronicler is tracing descent through Ahaz, Hezekiah, and Manasseh, the line still running from David and Solomon.

Both traditions trace the royal line as the Chronicler gives it, name the Kings parallel without forcing every spelling or family link into one form, and leave uncertain identifications in the later names openly hedged.

verses.text: Amon his son, and Josiah his son.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Amon his son, and Josiah his son.” Amon and Josiah close the father-to-son chain of sitting kings in this list, corresponding to 2 Kings 21–23. Josiah’s sons will be named next, because the succession after him is no longer a single simple line.

Arminian readers keep the two names as the last regular steps of the pre-exilic chain, historical rather than typological.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also take the verse as the approach to the end of the kingdom period in this genealogy. Kings has already told those reigns; this list only situates them in the family.

Both traditions trace the royal line as the Chronicler gives it, name the Kings parallel without forcing every spelling or family link into one form, and leave uncertain identifications in the later names openly hedged.

verses.text: The sons of Josiah: the firstborn Johanan, the second Jehoiakim, the third Zedekiah, and the fourth Shallum.
verses.arminianNotes:
Josiah’s sons are “the firstborn Johanan, the second Jehoiakim, the third Zedekiah, and the fourth Shallum.” Kings, already drafted, narrates Jehoahaz, Jehoiakim, and Zedekiah as kings after Josiah and does not, in those reign narratives, give Johanan a reign. Shallum is often identified with Jehoahaz; that is a common reading and should remain hedged, not declared from this verse alone.

Arminian readers let all four names stand as this book’s record of Josiah’s sons, without rearranging them to match the royal sequence in Kings.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also name the Kings parallel and keep the identifications cautious. Johanan, Jehoiakim, Zedekiah, and Shallum are listed in this order, and the next verse will continue from Jehoiakim.

Both traditions trace the royal line as the Chronicler gives it, name the Kings parallel without forcing every spelling or family link into one form, and leave uncertain identifications in the later names openly hedged.

verses.text: The sons of Jehoiakim: Jeconiah his son, and Zedekiah his son.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The sons of Jehoiakim: Jeconiah his son, and Zedekiah his son.” Jeconiah is the name this chapter uses for the king called Jehoiachin in 2 Kings 24, already drafted. Zedekiah here is called Jehoiakim’s son; the Zedekiah who reigned after Jeconiah is, in Kings, a son of Josiah, Jeconiah’s uncle. Whether verse 16 uses “son” in a dynastic sense, or names another Zedekiah, is not settled by the wording, and a harmony should not be forced.

Arminian readers report both the naming difference and the uncertain second name.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise leave Jeconiah/Jehoiachin as the two books’ forms, and they do not decide the Zedekiah question beyond what this short verse can bear.

Both traditions trace the royal line as the Chronicler gives it, name the Kings parallel without forcing every spelling or family link into one form, and leave uncertain identifications in the later names openly hedged.

verses.text: The sons of Jeconiah, the captive: Shealtiel his son,
verses.arminianNotes:
“The sons of Jeconiah, the captive: Shealtiel his son,” The title “the captive” marks Jeconiah’s exile, the setting already told in 2 Kings 24. Shealtiel is named as his son, and further names will follow in the next verse. From here the identifications become less certain, and later books will not always describe these relationships in the same way.

Arminian readers take the captive and Shealtiel as the text states them, and they will not yet settle every later question about this house.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also begin the post-exilic stretch with restraint. The royal line is still being named, now on the far side of the captivity, and the following verses will need the same caution.

Both traditions trace the royal line as the Chronicler gives it, name the Kings parallel without forcing every spelling or family link into one form, and leave uncertain identifications in the later names openly hedged.

verses.text: Malchiram, Pedaiah, Shenazzar, Jekamiah, Hoshama, and Nedabiah.
verses.arminianNotes:
Six further names follow Shealtiel: Malchiram, Pedaiah, Shenazzar, Jekamiah, Hoshama, and Nedabiah. The verse does not repeat the word “sons,” but it stands under the heading of verse 17. How each man is related to Jeconiah or to Shealtiel is not spelled out beyond this listing, and identifications should be hedged.

Arminian readers refuse to invent a precise family tree the names themselves do not supply.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers keep the six as the Chronicler’s own continuation of Jeconiah’s house, without forcing later identifications, including those sometimes proposed for Shenazzar, onto this line.

Both traditions trace the royal line as the Chronicler gives it, name the Kings parallel without forcing every spelling or family link into one form, and leave uncertain identifications in the later names openly hedged.

verses.text: The sons of Pedaiah: Zerubbabel and Shimei. The sons of Zerubbabel: Meshullam and Hananiah; and Shelomith was their sister;
verses.arminianNotes:
“The sons of Pedaiah: Zerubbabel and Shimei. The sons of Zerubbabel: Meshullam and Hananiah; and Shelomith was their sister;” This chapter makes Zerubbabel a son of Pedaiah. Other books, including Ezra and Haggai, call Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel. The difference should be named and left standing, not resolved by a levirate or adoptive theory the present verses do not state. The next names, including Shelomith their sister, belong to this record and are not all easy to identify elsewhere.

Arminian readers hold the two descriptions of Zerubbabel’s father side by side, as differences among the books.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hedge the relationship. Zerubbabel is central in the return, and this genealogy places him under Pedaiah; that placement is not to be erased for the sake of another book’s wording.

Both traditions trace the royal line as the Chronicler gives it, name the Kings parallel without forcing every spelling or family link into one form, and leave uncertain identifications in the later names openly hedged.

verses.text: and Hashubah, Ohel, Berechiah, Hasadiah, and Jushab Hesed, five.
verses.arminianNotes:
Five more names are added: “Hashubah, Ohel, Berechiah, Hasadiah, and Jushab Hesed, five.” They appear to continue Zerubbabel’s children after Meshullam, Hananiah, and Shelomith, though the verse itself only counts five. Identifications of these five should remain uncertain where later books do not clearly name them.

Arminian readers take the five as this list’s own addition to Zerubbabel’s house, a historical notice rather than a set of types.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise decline to assign later careers to names the verse only lists. The royal line after the exile is being counted, still with modest claims.

Both traditions trace the royal line as the Chronicler gives it, name the Kings parallel without forcing every spelling or family link into one form, and leave uncertain identifications in the later names openly hedged.

verses.text: The sons of Hananiah: Pelatiah and Jeshaiah; the sons of Rephaiah, the sons of Arnan, the sons of Obadiah, the sons of Shecaniah.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The sons of Hananiah: Pelatiah and Jeshaiah; the sons of Rephaiah, the sons of Arnan, the sons of Obadiah, the sons of Shecaniah.” After two named sons of Hananiah, the wording shifts to a series of “the sons of” without a clear father-to-son chain. That abrupt syntax is a real difficulty already visible in the WEB text; it should be noted neutrally, without claims about other manuscripts not inspected here. Identifications in this stretch remain uncertain.

Arminian readers will not invent a smooth pedigree the English wording does not give.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also leave the four “sons of” phrases as the list states them, a compact and difficult close to Hananiah’s verse, not a problem to be hidden or over-explained.

Both traditions trace the royal line as the Chronicler gives it, name the Kings parallel without forcing every spelling or family link into one form, and leave uncertain identifications in the later names openly hedged.

verses.text: The son of Shecaniah: Shemaiah. The sons of Shemaiah: Hattush, Igal, Bariah, Neariah, and Shaphat, six.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The son of Shecaniah: Shemaiah. The sons of Shemaiah: Hattush, Igal, Bariah, Neariah, and Shaphat, six.” Five names are given, and the total is six. The wording is left as it stands.

Arminian readers report the five names and the figure six as the text gives them.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same neutral stance. The difficulty is in the wording, and identifications of these sons should remain hedged.

Both traditions trace the royal line as the Chronicler gives it and leave this wording difficulty unresolved.

verses.text: The sons of Neariah: Elioenai, Hizkiah, and Azrikam, three.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The sons of Neariah: Elioenai, Hizkiah, and Azrikam, three.” Three sons are named, and the number matches the list. They belong to the later, uncertain stretch of the royal family, and should not be identified with better-known men of similar names unless a text actually does so.

Arminian readers take the three as a clear, modest genealogical step, still without a narrative.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same brief register. Neariah’s three sons continue the line as far as this chapter will take it, one generation at a time.

Both traditions trace the royal line as the Chronicler gives it, name the Kings parallel without forcing every spelling or family link into one form, and leave uncertain identifications in the later names openly hedged.

verses.text: The sons of Elioenai: Hodaviah, Eliashib, Pelaiah, Akkub, Johanan, Delaiah, and Anani, seven.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The sons of Elioenai: Hodaviah, Eliashib, Pelaiah, Akkub, Johanan, Delaiah, and Anani, seven.” Seven names close the chapter, and the number matches. These men are commonly read as among the latest Davidic names in the book, likely in the post-exilic period, but precise dates and identifications should remain hedged. The list that began with Adam has now been carried, through Israel and David, this far.

Arminian readers take the seven as the Chronicler’s last word in this royal genealogy, a real family close, not an allegory of completeness.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also refuse to force later identifications or a firm date on Anani and his brothers. The opening genealogies end with David’s line still named among Israel’s families, which has been the shared purpose of these chapters.

Both traditions trace the royal line as the Chronicler gives it, name the Kings parallel without forcing every spelling or family link into one form, and leave uncertain identifications in the later names openly hedged.
